Researching Information-Management-Systems [[]], Information-Science [[181]]

In a highly complex interlinked nonlinear system, i.e., Wikipedia [[221]] or Zettelkasten [89](89.md), how is knowledge organized such that it scales well into thousands of articles, or in the case of a graph-driven workflow, thousands of "nodes". Forming almost a "topology" [145](145.md) of knowledge; where some ideas are larger in mass (inlinks, cross-references, content-size, access-rate, relevance, etc.)

I'm assuming certain ideas emerge by necessity, suggesting "types" or "classes" of information and knowledge, just purely by necessities of structural management. This is perhaps where we see the emergence of "disambiguation" links in Wikipedia, and "Topic-hubs" in the zettelkasten approach.

However; the question remains; are these systems too vast for human management? The Greeks for example; only had analog methodologies for knowledge and study; yet their work far exceeded into the future; and much of our very own English language, rests on the backbone laid by the Greeks; whom themselves where inspired by and referenced preceeding languages.

This historical artifact of evolution naturally forms a "story"; an ontological record of experience. However, a story requires categorial structure; becuase language is structural. From graphemes, to words, to phrases, to sentences, paragraphs, sections, etc. This suggests Hierarchies are an inescapable, natural structure.

This makes the problem of systems management and sustainability even more cumbersome. These complex systems...

Almost resembling a "synthetic neural network, specialized in knowledge." Real neural networks are far more complex than "managing tags." However; neuroscience research is deeply relevant in this neighborhood of information-science. Speaking of "neighborhoods" coordinates and addresses are, in large, one of the only sources of "real-life links" that genuinely connect an otherwise nonlinear, complex world.

This is clearly visible in the Zettelkasten, where each note is assigned an "ID", acting as almost a linkable coordinate in space.

However, beyond the architectural semantics of each sysytem; the pragmatics problem remains; is a nonlinear-graph approach to knowledge, more prone to Entropy, than classical hierarchical systems?

Fascinatingly; the Human Brain contains both; Hierarchical architecture aswell as Nonlinear networks; and I suspect it is not merely an anatomical constraint; the evolved structures of knowledge systems almost always eventually point towards the "network" structure; yet it always requires Hierarchical assignment due to the problem of power distribution in a vast system.

Now this is getting complex; so let's zoom back out into the main topic.
